Part 1: Political party accountability project

Claude (chat, later Cowork)

Turn 1

We have been asked to make projects in the field of AI or Data Science or use spec-driven development to make it for a course in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence. I am considering the idea of building a political party accountability page, which scrapes news and past achievements and compares them against their manifesto. I shall be focusing on parties from Tamil Nadu and the past 15-20 years. Let's also score their past scandals and rate their favorability as ruling / opposition parties. Discuss this idea in further depth with me before I make a decision on whether to pursue this idea or not. Discuss the scope of this idea, how useful it is, how it can be made even stronger, and the weight it would carry in a course project. This is one of 4 required projects, and I am thinking of using this as the 2nd or 3rd best project. Cut out all flowery praise in your response

Claude's response

Here's my assessment.

The core problem with the idea as stated

It's really three projects bundled together, and they don't carry equal value:

  1. Manifesto vs. delivery tracking. This is the strongest part, and the only one that's real data science.
  2. Scandal scoring. This is the weakest part and the riskiest one.
  3. Ruling/opposition favorability rating. This one isn't defined yet. Favorability could mean public opinion, which needs survey data you don't have (Lokniti-CSDS, C-Voter). Or it could mean a performance index you compute yourself, which is just your weighting choices shown as a number.

There's also a logic gap. Only the governing party can be judged against its manifesto. AIADMK's 2021 promises can't be fulfilled or broken, because they didn't govern. PMK, NTK, VCK and TVK have never run the state government. So "compare all parties against their manifestos" collapses to the ruling party in each term. In practice that means DMK for 2006 and 2021, and AIADMK for 2011 and 2016. Opposition parties need a different yardstick. That could be assembly participation, the questions they raised, or whether they backed policies they had opposed. The data for that is thinner.

Scope

You'd be covering five election cycles (2006, 2011, 2016, 2021, 2026). Each manifesto has hundreds of promises, mostly in Tamil, often as scanned PDFs. Matching every promise to evidence across 20 years, by hand or by machine, is a semester-long project on its own. For one of four projects, that's too much.

A realistic core would be the DMK 2021 manifesto (a full term, now complete) plus AIADMK 2011 or 2016 for comparison. Do those deeply instead of covering everything shallowly.

Hard problems you'd have to solve

  • Fulfillment isn't binary. Take DMK's 2021 promise of ₹1,000/month to women heads of families. It launched in September 2023 as Kalaignar Magalir Urimai Thogai, two years late, with eligibility filters instead of universal coverage. Is that fulfilled, partial or diluted? You need a status rubric (fulfilled / partial / delayed / diluted / blocked externally / not started) and it has to be applied consistently.
  • Attribution. The NEET exemption promise was blocked at the Union/Presidential level. Counting it as the state government's failure is a judgment call your rubric has to make explicit.
  • Vague promises. "Improve healthcare infrastructure" can't be checked. You need to classify promises by specificity first and only score the measurable ones. That classification is itself a useful output.
  • News source bias. Tamil Nadu media is unusually tied to parties. Sun TV and Dinakaran are linked to the Maran family, close to DMK; Kalaignar TV is DMK's; Jaya TV and Namadhu Amma are AIADMK's. Scraping news without modeling the source skews your results. Government primary sources are better evidence: departmental policy notes (published every year), budget speeches, Governor's addresses, Government Orders and CAG reports. Use news as secondary evidence.
  • Scraping constraints. Paywalls, terms of service and robots.txt on major outlets. GDELT is a legitimate fallback for news metadata.

Scandal scoring: drop it or reframe it

A numeric scandal score fails for several reasons:

  • Legal outcomes flip. The 2G accused were acquitted in 2017, and the CBI's appeal is still pending. Jayalalithaa's disproportionate assets case went from conviction (2014) to High Court acquittal (2015) to the Supreme Court restoring the conviction (2017), though by then the case against her had abated because she had died. Where on a 1–10 scale does that go?
  • Weights are subjective. How much should an FIR count against a chargesheet against a conviction? How does ₹100 crore compare with ₹10,000 crore? How close was the person to the party leadership? Every choice is your opinion, and a composite score hides that.
  • Legal exposure. Criminal defamation still exists in India under BNS s.356. Publishing "Party X scandal score: 8.2" is riskier than publishing a sourced timeline.
  • Grading risk. An evaluator who sees it as partisan may mark down the whole project.

Better version: a sourced ledger of cases with categorical legal status (alleged / chargesheeted / convicted / acquitted / on appeal), dates and links. No composite score. If you want a number anyway, let users set the weights themselves so it's clearly their judgment, not yours.

How to make it stronger

What turns this from "scraper plus dashboard" into a DS/AI project is the pipeline plus evaluation:

  1. Ingestion. OCR for Tamil PDFs (Tesseract with the Tamil model, or a vision LLM), then split the text into individual promises.
  2. Classification. Sector, specificity (measurable or not), type (welfare transfer, infrastructure, policy/legal, freebie).
  3. Evidence retrieval. Retrieval over government documents and news using multilingual embeddings that handle Tamil. Compare BM25, dense retrieval and hybrid as an ablation.
  4. Status judgment. An LLM judge assigns a status with cited evidence and a confidence level. Low-confidence cases go to human review.
  5. Evaluation (the part most students skip). Hand-label 150–200 promises as a gold set. Have a second person label them too, and report inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa). Measure the pipeline's precision and recall against the gold set, and do error analysis. This is what earns marks.

Analyses that would be original rather than descriptive:

  • Promise recycling. Use semantic similarity across 2011, 2016, 2021 and 2026 manifestos to find promises that keep reappearing, which signals they were never delivered. This is cheap to build and makes a good headline finding.
  • Spending vs. promises. Do budget allocations by sector follow manifesto emphasis?
  • Specificity over time. Are manifestos getting vaguer or more concrete? What share of each manifesto is freebies, and is that trending up or down?

Usefulness

For the public: modest. A promise tracker for Tamil Nadu with this rigor doesn't really exist; PRS and Factly cover pieces of it. But most people won't use a student tool, and you'd have to maintain it to stay credible.

As a course and portfolio piece, it's more useful. It shows NLP on a low-resource language, retrieval, LLM-as-judge with evaluation, and handling messy real-world documents. That combination is less common than the usual Kaggle-style projects.

Weight in the course

  • Done as the narrowed pipeline plus evaluation: strong. It could reasonably be your best project, not just 2nd or 3rd.
  • Done as scraping, LLM summaries and a scoring dashboard: weak. It reads as a web app with opinions, and the political angle draws extra scrutiny.
  • Spec-driven framing: it fits naturally. The promise schema, status rubric and scoring rules are exactly the kind of thing you write a spec for before building.

Compared with your taxi ETA idea, this has a practical edge on data access: manifestos and government documents are public. Ola, Uber and Rapido have no public ETA data, so you'd have to collect your own over weeks.

Recommendation

Pursue it, but as a manifesto promise tracker for the ruling party in two terms, with a rigorous evaluation section. Replace scandal scoring with a sourced legal-status ledger, and drop "favorability" unless you can define it with real data.

How much time do you have for this project, and is it solo or a team? That decides whether two terms is realistic or whether you should start with just DMK 2021.

Turn 2

We can also cut down the timeframe to just 2016 and 2021, if the qty of documents are huge. I also want to add time until each promise is realised as a feature. This will help us compare governments in the middle of their ruling period. Ideally, I want to train a model which learns how promises are usually met over time using completed governments and predict how far the current TVK govt (elected in 2026) will go if they continue at this rate. I know this is a slight shift from the original idea, but see if this can be added in

Claude's response

Yes, this can be added. The prediction part is the strongest addition so far. Here's how it changes the project and where I'd push back.

Evaluation isn't the same as training

A hand-labeled set used only for testing doesn't put your opinions into the model. Its job is to tell you whether the LLM's verdicts are any good.

That matters more now. The time-to-realisation model learns from the LLM's status and date labels, so if those are wrong, the predictive model learns noise and nobody can tell. You don't need 200 labels:

  • 60–80 promises, labeled against a written rubric (fulfilled means a scheme was launched or a Government Order issued, not "I think they did well"). The rubric is what keeps the labels from being opinion.
  • A second annotator labels 30 of those, so you can report agreement. A teammate works best. Using a different LLM as the second labeler is weaker but acceptable.
  • Report the LLM judge's accuracy on status and its error in days on dates.

That's roughly a weekend of work, and it makes every downstream number defensible.

Non-measurable promises as the MVP: reframe it

A vague promise like "improve healthcare infrastructure" has no ground truth, so retrieval can find related actions but can't decide fulfilled vs. not. If that's the MVP, its output can't be scored.

The fix, which is also a good AI contribution, is promise decomposition. The LLM turns each vague promise into 2–4 checkable indicators. For the healthcare example, that could be new primary health centres, hospital beds added, and health's share of the budget. Retrieval then finds evidence per indicator, and the promise's status is the fraction of its indicators that were met. That gives you a status you can score, and it handles the hard case you care about.

Time to realisation: this is survival analysis

This is the right framing, and it's a standard DS method, which helps the project's academic weight.

  • Event: the promise is realised. You need one fixed definition of the date, such as the first GO or the scheme launch date. Budget announcements don't count. GO dates and launch dates are well documented, so this is the most extractable field you have.
  • Censoring: promises not realised by the end of a term aren't "infinite time". They're right-censored, and survival models handle that properly.
  • Models:
  • Kaplan–Meier curves per government give you the mid-term comparison directly. For example: "by month 18, AIADMK 2016 had realised X%, DMK 2021 Y%."
  • A Cox proportional hazards model (or a gradient-boosted survival model) predicts per-promise timing from covariates: sector, type (cash transfer / infrastructure / legislation), estimated cost, specificity, whether it needs Union approval, and whether it was a headline promise.

Predicting TVK's trajectory

It's feasible. The caveats belong in the report:

  • Only two completed governments in your window: AIADMK 2016–21 and DMK 2021–26. At the promise level you'll have several hundred observations, which is enough to train on. At the government level, n=2, so "how governments behave" is really "how these two behaved".
  • Both training terms had shocks. Jayalalithaa died in December 2016 and the leadership changed. COVID hit 2020–21. You could include a COVID-period indicator in the model.
  • TVK is a first-time government with no track record, which is a real distribution shift.
  • About five months of TVK data so far. "At this rate" extrapolation from that is thin. Your model shouldn't extrapolate TVK's own rate. It should apply the learned per-promise timing to TVK's manifesto, then update as realisations come in. Present projections as ranges, not point estimates.

The best part: backtesting is your automatic evaluation, with no manual work. Train on the 2016 term, give the model the first 6/12/24 months of the 2021 term, predict the rest, and compare against what actually happened. If it predicts DMK's final outcome reasonably from early data, the TVK projection has credibility. If it doesn't, that's an honest and gradeable finding too.

If the document volume allows, add 2011–16 as a third training term, even with lighter coverage. Going from two governments to three noticeably strengthens the model.

Revised project shape

  1. Extract promises from the 2016, 2021 and 2026 manifestos (English versions).
  2. Classify and decompose: sector, type, specificity; vague promises become indicators.
  3. Retrieve evidence: policy notes, GOs, budget speeches, news. Output: status plus realisation date, with citations.
  4. Validate: a 60–80 promise test set and the agreement score.
  5. Model: survival curves per government, a hazard model, the 2016→2021 backtest, and a TVK projection with uncertainty bands.
  6. Dashboard: cumulative-realisation curves aligned by month-in-term, so governments compare at the same point in their tenure.

Scandal scoring and favorability are now out, which helps the scope.

As a course project this is now clearly above "2nd or 3rd best". It has NLP, retrieval, LLM-as-judge with validation, survival modeling and a forecast backtested on real outcomes. The main risk is time, and nearly all of it sits in step 3. Build steps 1–3 for the 2021 term alone first, before you scale up.

Turn 3

Yeah retrieving the evidence part, can we handle it with a simple scraping tool? I think govt. websites won't oppose this. Or would I need to download all documents locally for BM25 to run on?

Claude's response

You need both. Scraping is how you collect the documents, and BM25 (or any retrieval method) then runs on a local index built from them. BM25 can't search live websites: it needs the full text in hand to compute term statistics. So it's two stages:

  1. Collect once: crawl the government sites, download the PDFs and pages, extract the text, and store it with metadata (department, date, document type).
  2. Search locally: index that text, then run every promise as a query against the index.

Why not search live per promise?

You could send each promise to a web search API instead of building a corpus. For this project that's worse:

  • Not reproducible. Search results change over time, so your backtest and evaluation numbers won't hold still.
  • Rate limits and cost across hundreds of promises, times several decomposed indicators each.
  • Missing dates. Live results don't reliably give you the document date, and the date is the most important field for time-to-realisation.

A local corpus is also small. Policy notes for about 40–50 departments over 10 years come to roughly 500 PDFs, plus about 10 budget speeches, about 10 Governor's addresses, and a filtered subset of GOs. That's a few GB of PDFs and much less as extracted text, which fits comfortably on a laptop.

Government sites in practice

Permission isn't the problem. These are public documents, and polite crawling is fine: rate-limit to about 1 request per second, check robots.txt, and cache so you never fetch anything twice. The real problems are practical:

  • Documents disappear after a change of government. Sites get restructured and older documents are often removed. For 2016–21 material, the Wayback Machine (archive.org) is often your only source. Check this early.
  • Slow, flaky servers and inconsistent URLs. Build retries into the crawler and log every failure.
  • Some scanned PDFs, even in English. Use PyMuPDF or pdfplumber first, with OCR as a fallback only when a page has no text layer.
  • GO repositories are huge. Filter them by department and date range instead of downloading everything.

News sites are a different matter: paywalls and terms of service restrict scraping. Keep news to a small secondary source, using GDELT for metadata or a few outlets with accessible archives.

Retrieval: use hybrid, not just BM25

Promise wording rarely matches government wording. "₹1,000 monthly to women heads of families" became "Kalaignar Magalir Urimai Thogai" in the GOs, and BM25 will miss that match. So:

  • BM25 (rank_bm25 is enough at this size) catches exact terms: scheme names, amounts, places.
  • Embeddings (FAISS or Chroma) catch paraphrases.
  • LLM query expansion rewrites each promise or indicator into 3–4 phrasings, including likely scheme names, before searching.
  • Reranking: merge the two result lists, then pass the top 10–20 chunks to the LLM judge.

This also gives you the BM25-vs-dense-vs-hybrid comparison from earlier almost for free.

Suggested stack

  • Crawling: requests + BeautifulSoup for most sites. Use Playwright only where a site needs JavaScript.
  • Storage: raw files on disk, plus a SQLite table with one row per document (URL, department, date, type, file path).
  • Chunking: split documents into passages of about 300–500 words, each keeping its document's metadata.

Build the crawler for one source first: the 2021–26 policy notes. They're the densest evidence for the DMK term and will show you most of the site quirks before you scale up.

Turn 4

Are there any more parts we need to discuss before we head on to the actual building?

Claude's response

Yes. A few decisions are cheaper to make now than to fix halfway through the build.

1. Write the spec first

These definitions drive everything downstream, so write them down before any code:

  • What counts as one promise. Manifestos bundle things: "free bus travel for women and students, and 1,000 new buses" is two or three promises. Decide how to split them, and how to handle the same promise appearing in two sections.
  • The status rubric, with the exact evidence needed for each status (fulfilled / partial / diluted / delayed / blocked externally / not started).
  • The realisation date: which event counts (GO issued, scheme launched, or first disbursement). Pick one and apply it everywhere.
  • The record schema for each promise: ID, text, party, year, sector, type, specificity, indicators, status, date, evidence links, confidence.

This document also covers the spec-driven development angle for the course.

2. Leakage in the backtest

This is the most important technical risk.

  • The LLM already knows the answers. Any recent LLM has read news about DMK 2021–26. If it judges promises from memory instead of from your retrieved documents, the backtest is contaminated. Require every verdict to cite a chunk from your corpus, and reject verdicts with no citation.
  • The time cutoff. When you predict DMK's outcome from its first 12 months, the features and evidence must come only from documents dated before month 12. This is why document dates in your metadata matter.
  • Features known only in hindsight. "Headline promise" has to be judged from the manifesto or campaign coverage, not from what later got attention.

3. Survival model covariates

Decide the features now, because the LLM extracts them in the same pass as classification. Candidates: sector, promise type, cost band (low/medium/high), specificity, whether it needs Union government involvement, whether it continues an existing scheme, and whether it's a headline promise. Define each with a short rubric, the same way as the status labels.

4. LLM cost and consistency

A rough estimate: about 600 promises across three manifestos × 3 indicators × about 8k tokens of retrieved context per judgment ≈ 15M input tokens per full run, and you'll run it more than once.

  • Use a cheap model for extraction and classification, and a stronger one only for the final judgment.
  • Cache every LLM response, keyed by prompt plus model version, so reruns cost nothing.
  • Use temperature 0, store prompts in the repo, and record the model version with each verdict. Otherwise results drift between runs and you can't reproduce your own numbers.

Check what API credits you have, or whether the course provides any, before choosing models.

5. Neutrality

Apply the same rubric, prompts and thresholds to every party, and state that in the report and on the dashboard. Show evidence links next to every status so users can check the verdict. Frame the TVK output as "projection under historical patterns", not "TVK will fail to deliver X%". This also protects you if an evaluator reads it as partisan.

6. Deliverables and scope cut-offs

  • What the course needs: report, demo, repo, presentation? Build toward that list, not a polished product.
  • A minimal dashboard: Streamlit is enough. Don't spend time on frontend work.
  • A fallback plan in advance: if time runs short, drop indicator decomposition for vague promises and keep only specific ones. Drop the TVK projection before the backtest, since the backtest is what gives the projection meaning.

7. Team and timeline

Who owns which stage (crawler, extraction, retrieval/judge, modeling), and the milestones: corpus done → 2021 term judged → evaluation set → model → dashboard.

Build order once those are settled: spec → crawler for 2021–26 policy notes → promise extraction for DMK 2021 → retrieval and judge on 20 promises → check them by hand → scale up.

What's your deadline, and is this solo or with a team? That decides how much of sections 3 and 6 stays in scope.

One line per settled decision: ID · date · decision · reason. Settled decisions are not reopened without a new entry.

- **D-001 · 2026-10-05 · Only ruling parties are analysed.** Only a governing party can fulfil a manifesto.
- **D-002 · 2026-10-05 · No scandal, favourability or composite party scores.** They hide subjective weights, carry defamation risk and invite bias accusations.
- **D-003 · 2026-10-06 · Terms:** DMK 2021–26 (training), AIADMK 2016–21 (backtest target), TVK 2026– (projection). AIADMK 2011–16 only if time allows.

I've read CLAUDE.md, STATUS.md, the decision log and the global spec. I also checked the machine's environment, without changing anything. I haven't written any files or opened the manifestos. I only looked at their filenames.

What I found first

  • Spec filename: the file is specs/00-global-spec.md (hyphens). I'll name the new one specs/01-corpus-collection.md to match.
  • Manifesto filenames don't match STATUS. STATUS asks for DMK-2021_ta.pdf, but the files are named like DMK_2021-ta.pdf. Present: DMK 2021 (en + ta), AIADMK 2016 (ta only), TVK 2026 (ta only, 30 MB). Under §3.1, DMK uses the English version and the other two use Tamil.
  • Tesseract has no tam language pack. Only eng and osd are installed. §3.1 and D-014 need tam.
  • Network: PyPI, tn.gov.in, cms.tn.gov.in and web.archive.org are reachable. tnbudget.tn.gov.in and cag.gov.in time out, so budget speeches and CAG reports would have to come through the Wayback Machine or be downloaded by you.
  • Python 3.10.12 is installed, as are pdftotext and git (2 commits so far).

Plan for stage 01, following the §12.1 template

Purpose. Build the foundation code, and collect, date, parse and chunk the English government evidence for 2016–26 (plus the start of 2026–). Finish with a coverage report that shows the gaps early (§13).

Part A: foundation code (STATUS says stage 01 builds it) - config/settings.yaml: the terms (§7 terms), paths and thresholds (chunk size, OCR trigger, crawl rate). config/sources.yaml: the source list. - src/ept/schema.py: pydantic v2 models that mirror all of §7 and the §8 enum. They import from the spec and redefine nothing. - src/ept/db.py: SQLite at data/ept.sqlite, rebuildable, with idempotent upserts. - src/ept/llm.py: the interface, prompt loading with a version: header, JSON-schema validation with one retry, a cache keyed on backend + model + prompt version + input hash, a usage log, and mock mode (EPT_LLM_MOCK=1). The real bulk backend stays a stub until spec 02 (Q-03). - CLI with typer: python -m ept crawl | parse | coverage, each with --term, --limit and --force. - Run metadata in reports/runs/{run_id}.json (§9.4).

Part B: corpus collection - Inputs: the source list for each doc_type (policy_note, budget_speech, governor_address, go, cag_report, scheme_page, news) and the date window for each term. - crawl: walk the official listing pages on a fixed schedule. It is rate-limited, respects robots.txt and sends an identifying user-agent. Files are stored once and never changed, at data/raw/evidence/{doc_type}/{doc_id}.{ext}. Each gets a sha256, fetched_at, and archive_url when the copy came from or is backed by Wayback. Re-runs skip files already fetched. - Dating: a rule for each document type gives doc_date + date_precision, plus fiscal_year. The date comes from the source's own metadata or the document's front matter. Anything left undated stays undated, and later cutoff runs leave it out. - parse: PyMuPDF text. A page with too little text gets Tesseract eng and parse_status=ocr. HTML goes through BeautifulSoup. A document detected as Tamil is flagged and not chunked, since Tamil evidence is out of scope (§3). - chunk: ~300–500 words, keeping page_start/page_end, with doc_date copied onto each chunk and the {doc_id}-{seq:04d} id format. - Manifestos: registered in documents as doc_type=manifesto with their hashes, and never chunked into the evidence pool. - Coverage report (reports/coverage_01.md + JSON): counts by doc_type × fiscal year × department, % dated by precision, parse status, OCR share, and an explicit list of gaps.

Leakage warning (rules that apply in this stage) - Rule 2: dates must be reliable, and an undated document is never assigned a guessed date. - Manifestos are kept out of the evidence chunks, so no promise can count as evidence for itself. - Sources are selected by systematic crawls of listings. No hand-picking pages because we know a scheme was delivered, which is the stage-01 version of rule 6. - No LLM is used in stage 01, so model memory can't affect what goes into the corpus.

Acceptance criteria and tests (draft) - Offline pytest with fixture HTML/PDF: deterministic doc_ids, the date parser for each type, chunk boundaries and word counts, the OCR-trigger decision, an idempotent second run, and mock round-trips for schema, db and llm. - A --limit 20 real run checked by hand, then the full run plus the coverage report.

Out of scope: promise extraction and Tamil OCR of manifestos (stage 02, Q-10), indexing and embeddings (stage 04), Tamil evidence.

Decisions I need from you before drafting the spec

  1. Q-01, term dates. For AIADMK-2016 I believe swearing-in was 2016-05-23 and the term ended when DMK was sworn in on 2021-05-07. Both dates need confirming from an official source. I don't reliably know TVK's 2026 swearing-in date or DMK's term end, so please give me those or a source for them. Also: should term_end be the day before the next swearing-in, and do CM changes within AIADMK-2016 count as the same term? I'd say yes to both.
  2. Q-02, source scope given 2 days (days 3–4). Which doc_types are essential for stage 01? My suggestion: policy notes, budget speeches, Governor's addresses and CAG reports first. Then scheme pages. GOs come last, and only for departments that match manifesto sectors, because the GO volume runs to thousands a year. Should news be left out of stage 01 entirely?
  3. Unreachable sites. Should budget speeches and CAG reports come through Wayback, or will you download them and drop them into a folder? Should a Wayback capture date be allowed as a fallback doc_date (date_precision=day, marked as an upper bound)? It is never earlier than the true date, so it's safe for cutoffs, though it is conservative.
  4. Manifesto handling in stage 01. Should stage 01 only register the manifestos and leave all text extraction and OCR to stage 02 (my recommendation)? Or should it parse them now, as the day plan's "Corpus: manifestos" suggests?
  5. Manifesto filenames. Should I rename the files to the STATUS convention or update STATUS to match the existing names? Renaming is cheap now and gets harder later.
  6. Tesseract tam. It's needed by stage 02 at the latest. Can you install the Tamil language pack on your Mac (for example, brew install tesseract-lang), or should I try installing it here?
  7. Evidence window. I'd use 2016-05-01 to today. Pre-term documents (for example, the AIADMK 2016 budget before the election) count only as context and can't support a realisation, since §7 requires a realisation date on or after sworn_in. OK?

Once you've answered these, I'll draft specs/01-corpus-collection.md and bring it back for approval before any code.

The draft spec is at specs/01-corpus-collection.md, marked DRAFT v0.1. I renamed the four manifestos to DMK-2021_en.pdf, DMK-2021_ta.pdf, AIADMK-2016_ta.pdf and TVK-2026_ta.pdf. Nothing is committed and no code is written yet.

How I set it up for Claude Code - The spec has an 11-step build order, each step with a command to check it and a git commit point. - It lists every config key, module, test file and fixture. - It names the cases where Claude Code must stop and ask you. - Every command gets a --time-budget flag, because each command Claude runs on your machine is cut off after about 3 minutes. Long crawls therefore run in short slices or in the background and pick up where they left off.

What I found while probing the sites - GOs: tn.gov.in lists them by department and year back to 2002, each with its date, GO number and subject. Filenames mark the language (_e_ for English, _t_ for Tamil), which makes pairing English and Tamil versions easy. - Gaps in the GO listings: Health has 0 GOs listed for 2017 and 37 for 2022, against 278 for 2019. The coverage report flags gaps like these. - Budget speeches: tnbudget.tn.gov.in is only reachable through Wayback, which has the 2021-22 to 2025-26 speeches. I couldn't find the 2016-17 to 2020-21 speeches, Governor's addresses after 2009, or CAG reports yet. - Third-party trackers exist but are uneven: South First covers 505 DMK promises, while TNM's AIADMK-2016 status check only covers some sectors.

Risks you should look at 1. Your tracker idea risks leakage and bias. Adding GOs because a tracker says a promise was delivered adds evidence based on known outcomes. Since DMK's tracker is much more complete, it would also add more of that evidence to DMK than to AIADMK, which skews the reverse backtest. The spec tags these documents (discovery=tracker_lead) so results can be reported with and without them. Tracker text itself never becomes evidence. This is OQ-3. 2. Partial dates need a fix in stage 04. A date known only to the month is stored as the 1st of that month, so a cutoff check against that stored date would let documents in up to a month early. The spec makes stage 04 compare against the end of the period instead. Documents with only a fiscal year stay undated rather than getting a made-up date. 3. Your Tamil Tesseract install isn't visible to Claude. Claude runs commands in a separate sandbox on your machine, and it still lists only English. This doesn't block stage 01, but stage 02 needs Tamil OCR (OQ-6).

Decisions I need from you (§9) - OQ-1: approve the global spec changes this needs: - Tamil evidence documents can be catalogued, but don't count as evidence until a later decision; - three new document fields (lang, date_source, discovery); - a rule for documents whose URL served different files over time; - two new folders. - OQ-2: how many GOs to download, decided once the dry run gives a real size and time estimate. - OQ-3: how to handle the tracker asymmetry, and whether you know of other trackers to add. - OQ-4: include Performance Budgets, skip Citizen Charters. - OQ-5: a 45-minute search for the missing sources, then a list of files for you to download by hand.

Once you've answered, I'll update the global spec to v0.4, log the decisions, mark spec 01 approved and commit it. Building would then start from step 1.

--- old
- If one URL served **different files over time** (distinct Wayback digests, e.g. the interim and revised 2021-22 budget at the same URL), each version after the first gets `doc_id = sha1(source_url + "@" + wayback_timestamp)`. This needs a §7 wording amendment (OQ-1).
+++ new
- If one URL served **different files over time** (distinct Wayback digests), keep **only the latest version**, which is treated as the updated document after modifications or revocations (user decision, 2026-10-07). This keeps one document per URL, so the §7 `doc_id` rule needs no change.
  - **Date safety:** the Wayback date fallback for that document uses the first capture **of the kept digest**, not the URL's first capture. The URL's first capture would date the newer file to the older file's timestamp, which is too early and leaks.
  - Superseded versions are not downloaded. They are listed (URL, digest, capture range) in the coverage report so nothing disappears silently. Known case: `BS_2021_22_*` served the AIADMK interim budget (Feb 2021) and later the DMK revised budget (Aug 2021). Only the revised one is kept.

I've updated specs/01-corpus-collection.md to v0.2 with your answers and real GO counts. It's still uncommitted and waiting on three questions at the end.

OQ-2: how many GOs. I counted every GO listing page (38 departments × 2016–2026), fetching only the HTML pages, no PDFs: - 7,051 GOs fall in the evidence window. That's far fewer than my earlier guess, because the site only publishes a subset of GOs. - They come to about 9 GB (average 1.3 MB per file); your disk has 204 GB free. - Filtering out routine orders like transfers and pensions would only cut about 11%, so I now recommend downloading all of them. - 100 of the 418 department-years are empty. Those will show up in the coverage report as gaps.

OQ-1: latest version. I've applied your rule: when the same web address held different files over time, only the newest file is kept. Two things come with it: - The fallback date for the kept file is taken from the first Wayback snapshot of that file. If it came from the first snapshot of the web address, the newer file would get the older file's date, which is too early and would leak. - The 2021-22 budget speech is one such case. That address first held AIADMK's interim budget (Feb 2021), then DMK's revised one (Aug 2021). We keep the revised one. The interim one is listed in the coverage report instead of being silently dropped.

OQ-3: trackers. You're right that they improve completeness, and that is exactly why they need a tag. If we find more DMK-era documents because DMK has a much fuller tracker, DMK will look better at delivering. That would come from more searching, not more delivery, and it would skew the DMK-vs-AIADMK comparison and the backtest. So I'm using them as you intended, and every document found through a tracker is tagged so we can check results with and without those documents. It costs almost nothing.

Leaving the laptop running won't keep long jobs going. I tested it: anything I start in the background is killed when my command returns, and each command can run for at most about 3 minutes. Downloading 9 GB from my side would take roughly 60–100 separate 3-minute runs, which is a lot of your Claude usage.

Still open: 1. OQ-1(b): add three fields to the documents table in the global spec? - lang: English or Tamil - date_source: where the date came from, which marks the Wayback dates you want to check by hand - discovery: how the document was found, which carries the tracker tag

If not, they can live in the per-file metadata sidecars instead, but later stages can't filter on them as easily. 2. OQ-2: download all ~7,050 English GOs? 3. OQ-7: I recommend that I build and test everything on small runs, and you then run one command in your Mac terminal for the big GO download (about 3–5 hours, and it can resume if interrupted). The alternative is that I run all the 3-minute slices myself.

Once you've answered, I'll update the global spec to v0.4, log the decisions, mark spec 01 approved, commit, and start build step 1.

Turn 13

What is expected from me in a spotcheck?

Claude's response

A spot-check is a short manual audit to confirm the pipeline isn't quietly getting things wrong. You open the actual documents and compare them with what the code recorded. It should take about 30–40 minutes for 20 documents.

How to make it easy: at step 8, ask Claude Code for a spot-check sheet first:

Pick 20 documents at random across all sources (at least 2 per doc_type) and write data/interim/spotcheck_01.csv with doc_id, local_path, source_url, doc_type, department, title, doc_date, date_precision, date_source, lang, parse_status, n_chunks and the first 150 words of chunk 1, plus empty columns ok_type, ok_date, ok_dept, ok_text and notes.

For each document, open the PDF and check:

  1. Type: is it really what doc_type says (a GO, policy note, budget speech, …)?
  2. Date: this is the most important check.
  3. If date_source is listing or document_text, the recorded date should match the date printed on the document. For a GO that's the date in its header. For a budget speech it's the "presented on" date.
  4. If it's wayback_capture or none, it doesn't have to be right. It only has to be flagged (present in date_review.csv).
  5. What fails: a confident date that's wrong, especially one that's too early, because that leaks into cutoff runs.
  6. Department: is it the right department? Small naming differences are fine.
  7. Text: does chunk 1 read as proper English text from this document? Watch for garbage characters, text from a different file, or a chunk that is mostly a table of numbers. If the PDF is a scan, was it OCR'd (parse_status = ocr) instead of coming out empty?

Mark each column Y or N, and add a note for anything odd.

Pass rule (spec §6, criterion 8): at least 18 of 20 have the right type and an acceptable date, meaning correct or correctly flagged. Any too-early date counts as a real problem even if 18/20 pass, so Claude Code should find out why it happened before the full run.

Afterwards: give the filled CSV back to Claude Code. It records the result in STATUS and fixes any pattern behind the failures, for example a date regex that picks up a cited GO's date instead of the document's own.

The step 4 pause is a smaller version of the same thing: 5 documents from one source, checked the same way. It's there to catch a broken date parser before the code is built out for every source.

Turn 15

How to check if first OCR chunk is readable?

Claude's response

Put the chunk text next to the PDF page it came from and compare. It takes about a minute.

1. Get the text up. The what_to_check column should say which page to open. For the chunk text itself, use whichever of these is easiest: - the excerpt in the CSV, if Claude Code included one; - the full extracted text at data/interim/text/{doc_id}.txt, where pages are separated by form-feed characters; - or in a terminal: sqlite3 data/ept.sqlite "select page_start, page_end, text from chunks where chunk_id='<doc_id>-0000';"

2. Open the PDF at page_start.

3. Mark it ok if: - you can read it as English sentences that match the page; - the important tokens survive: scheme names, amounts (Rs. 800 crore), GO numbers and dates are correct when you check two or three against the page; - the garbling is only scattered, roughly 1 bad word in 20 or fewer.

Mark it wrong if: - whole lines are symbol soup (~ |Il ;-') or it's mostly broken table fragments; - amounts or dates are mangled (800 → 8OO, 2019 → 2O19); - the text is from a different page or document than the PDF shows; - it's empty or nearly empty, though the page clearly has text; - the text is duplicated, for example the same page OCR'd twice.

Your current run has an example, from the Agriculture GO excerpt: "the Government _of India have released the ist instalment… NESM- Oilseeds". There, "ist" should be "1st" and "NESM" should be "NFSM". That's typical OCR noise and counts as ok. Searching for "National Food Security Mission oil seeds instalment" would still find it. The table that follows (Category wise GOI share… ~ General SIE St |Total |) is garbled, but that only matters if the table were the only place a key figure appears. Put that in note, not wrong.

Rule of thumb: ask yourself whether someone searching for this promise would find this chunk, and whether a judge reading it could tell what the GO does. If both answers are yes, it's ok.

If several OCR items come out borderline, tell Claude Code. It can raise the OCR resolution (DPI) or add an image clean-up step before re-running. Don't fix those by hand.

Turn 16

Will the crawl/parse take a toll on my internet connection. Explain briefly how the entire thing works

Claude's response

Network: light, but about 10 GB in total. - The crawler downloads one file at a time, about one request per second to each site, on purpose, so it doesn't hammer government servers. At those speeds it uses only part of a normal home broadband line. Video calls and browsing should still work, maybe a little slower while a big PDF is downloading. - The total is around 9–10 GB (about 7,000 GOs plus policy notes and the other documents), spread over several hours. - The one real concern is a data cap. If you're on a mobile hotspot or a capped plan, 10 GB matters. Run it on unmetered Wi-Fi. - If it does get in the way, the rate is a setting (http.rate_per_host in config/settings.yaml), so it can be slowed down. You can also stop with Ctrl-C at any time and re-run later. It resumes where it stopped and never downloads a file twice.

Parse: no internet, but heavy on the CPU. - Parsing works only on files already on your disk. - OCR is the costly part. In the 20-document run, 15 needed it, so most GOs are probably scans. OCR across thousands of documents could take many hours of CPU, with the fans running and the battery draining. Keep the laptop plugged in, and run it overnight if you can.

How the whole stage works:

  1. Catalogue. For each source (policy-note pages, GO listings, Wayback archives for the budget and CAG sites, scheme pages), the crawler reads the listing pages only. It writes down every document it finds, with its link, department, title, and the date from the listing if there is one. This part is small and fast.
  2. Fetch. It downloads each catalogued PDF. If the government site fails, it fetches the archived copy from the Wayback Machine instead. Each file is saved once, with its fingerprint (sha256) and a small sidecar file noting where it came from.
  3. Parse. It pulls the text out of each PDF. Pages with almost no text are scanned images, so those go through Tesseract OCR.
  4. Language check. Tamil documents are set aside, catalogued but not used as evidence.
  5. Dating. It picks the most trustworthy date available, in this order: the official listing, the date printed on the document, the filename, then the earliest Wayback snapshot. Weak dates go into date_review.csv for you. Dates that look impossible are flagged.
  6. Chunk. It splits the text into passages of about 400 words, keeping page numbers. These chunks are what later stages search and what the judge cites.
  7. Coverage report. It summarises what was collected by type, year and department, and lists the gaps.

Later stages never touch the internet for evidence. They work only from this local corpus, which is what keeps the judging leak-free.

It's stuck. The reason you see so little output is that the crawler only prints when it starts a source, never per file. Here's what actually happened overnight, all in the CAG step:

  • 00:38 to 06:25: it downloaded 12 of the 23 CAG reports. CAG's site only works through Wayback, which is slow, and these files are large (up to 62 MB), so each took 15–30 minutes.
  • Since 06:25: nothing. It's almost certainly stuck on one slow Wayback download. The 60-second timeout only fires when no data arrives at all, so a connection that trickles a few bytes now and then keeps it waiting forever.
  • The GOs never started. They come after CAG and the scheme pages in the source order.

A real bug also turned up. The last file it saved (cag_report/d3b27b7df46eabaf.pdf) is exactly 5,242,880 bytes, which is 5 MiB, and the PDF has no end marker. Wayback archived a cut-off copy. Because that cut-off copy has a different fingerprint from the earlier capture, the "keep the latest version" rule treated it as a newer edition and kept it over the 2024 capture, which may be complete. Truncated archive copies have to count as failures, not new versions.

What to do now:

  1. Press Ctrl-C. It's safe: every download is written to a temporary file first and only renamed when complete, and re-running skips whatever is already done.
  2. Start the GOs now so the night isn't wasted again: caffeinate -i python -m ept crawl --source tn_gos GOs come from the live tn.gov.in site, not Wayback, so they should move far faster.
  3. Give Claude Code this prompt:

The full crawl stalled for 3.5 h on a Wayback CAG download, with no output. Fix the following, add a test for each, and log the decision: 1. A per-file progress line: [n/N] source doc_id size time. 2. A total time limit per download (http.max_download_s in settings, e.g. 600). Implement it by streaming the download and aborting when the limit is passed, not only on a read timeout. A download that hits the limit counts as a retryable failure and goes into the coverage gap list. 3. A completeness check before keeping a PDF: it must contain %%EOF and open in PyMuPDF. A truncated Wayback capture is not a "newer version" under D-018. When choosing a version, ignore digests whose captures are truncated and fall back to the latest complete capture. If none is complete, record a fetch failure. 4. Scan the CAG files already downloaded for truncation. d3b27b7df46eabaf.pdf is exactly 5 MiB and has no %%EOF. Re-fetch or flag them. 5. Run the slow Wayback-only sources (CAG) last, after GOs and scheme pages.

class Budget:
    """--time-budget: commands check `expired()` between items and stop cleanly."""

    def __init__(self, seconds: Optional[float], clock=None):
        import time

        self._clock = clock or time.monotonic
        self.deadline = None if seconds is None else self._clock() + seconds

    def expired(self) -> bool:
        return self.deadline is not None and self._clock() >= self.deadline
EOF

  • First chunks: every first chunk is a cover page plus table of contents, e.g. "INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY DEPARTMENT POLICY NOTE 2016—2017 DEMAND NO. 31 … © Government of Tamil Nadu 2016 … INDEX …". Later chunks are clean prose.
  • Chunk sizes: 300–500 words; only each document's last chunk is shorter.
  • All 5 are ocr: each has at least one page under 200 characters (cover pages, charts). On two rotated landscape tables, Tesseract produced mirrored garbage, so a little noise gets into chunks.
  • Date review: all 5 are in date_review.csv. One flag is a false "anachronism": the text says "extended up to 30.04.2020", which is a future period, not a wrong date.

Findings that need your decision:

  1. Policy notes contain no issue date. Their front matter only has "POLICY NOTE 2017–2018" and "© Government of Tamil Nadu 2016".
  2. The files have almost no Wayback captures at their current address.
  3. The same files exist at the address the site used before it moved: cms.tn.gov.in/sites/default/files/documents/. Wayback has many captures there, and I checked 3 files: today's bytes match the earliest capture exactly (same digest). So the strict D-018 rule (first capture of the bytes we keep) works there.
  4. I added that address as an extra Wayback lookup. Only an exact byte match can set a date, so it can never date a different version. With it, 3 of the 5 are dated. This is the uncommitted change.
  5. The dates are conservative. For example, the IT 2016-17 note is dated 2017-07-22, about a year after it was tabled.
  6. The © year could date most of the rest. "© Government of Tamil Nadu 2016" could become a year-precision document_text date, so the note counts as available from 2016-12-31 onward.
  7. This is safe as long as the © year is the year it was published.
  8. The spec only allows day or month precision for text dates, so this would be a change to the spec.
  9. The policy-note listing has more than policy notes. The Finance and Public department pages also list:
  10. Budget speeches 2016-17 → 2026-27, including the 2016 interim/revised and the 2021 interim/revised;
  11. Governor's addresses from June 2016 to June 2026;
  12. Agriculture budget speeches, state sector policies (Data Centre 2021, Textile 2019, …), Local Fund Audit reports, and Commission of Inquiry reports.

That covers most of the S3 2016–21 and S4 gaps in the spec. Today they are catalogued but excluded, as the spec says for this source.

Two things I handled myself; tell me if you disagree: - --limit N means "the first N in-scope items per source" (in a fixed, spread-out order), not "N new downloads". It still caps new downloads at N. It's the only reading under which the step 3 check and acceptance criterion 2 both hold. - I'm running on your Mac directly, not in a Linux sandbox. I used .venv/ (Python 3.11); .venv-linux/ and the timeout 175 slices in §4.10 don't apply here, and macOS has no timeout command. Tesseract tam is already installed here, which also answers OQ-6. I haven't changed D-021; you still run the full download.

The new spot-check sheet is ready at data/interim/spotcheck_01.csv, with 10 rows from the existing --limit 20 run. The old spot_check_01.csv is deleted, and everything is committed as stage 01: spot-check sheet per D-027 (4d960fd). All 108 tests pass.

What's in the sheet: - Columns: exactly as §12.4 says: item_id, why_flagged, what_to_check, path, verdict, note. verdict and note are empty. - Spread: 3 GOs, 3 scheme pages, 2 CAG reports, 2 policy notes, so no source has more than 3. - Ranking: every row has a failed date check (anachronism, sometimes with an FY-mismatch or out-of-window flag as well). All of them outrank documents that are merely Wayback-dated, so no plain weak-date rows made the top 10. - what_to_check: each row names a page and the exact dates to compare. For example: "GO header should read Ms No.114 dated 23-07-2024 … Text p.1 mentions 04-09-2024 ('04.09.2024'), after the stored date: is it a future/target date (ok) or is the document really later (wrong)?" - path: the local file plus the source URL.

Changes I made to get there: - The sheet comes from a new command, python -m ept spotcheck, so it can be regenerated. Its limits (7–10 rows, max 3 per source) are in config/settings.yaml. - Spec 01, step 8: group (a) is now spelled out as anachronism, conflict, FY mismatch and out of window, ranked ahead of all weak dates. Group (b) no longer names a copyright_year date_source. It now says © year dates are stored as document_text and are recognised by kind = copyright in the sidecar, or the "dated from © year" reason in date_review.csv. I also added spotcheck to the CLI line and the sheet to the outputs table. - Global spec: §12.4 now comes after §12.3.

What to expect: - Progress lines: a line every 25 downloads for each source. When it reaches the GOs, there's first a few minutes of "reading listings" lines (one per 500 items), then download progress with an estimated time left. - When the crawl finishes: look at its last line before parse output starts scrolling. - crawl: done: all good; parse runs next. - crawl: stopped (...) or ... deferred: Wayback unavailable: let parse finish anyway. Then run the crawl again, and parse once more afterwards to pick up the extra files. - Don't start parse in a second terminal while the crawl is running. Both write to the same database, and running them side by side can cause "database is locked" errors. - Keep the Mac plugged in with the lid open. caffeinate -i stops it sleeping when idle, but closing the lid can still put it to sleep. If anything stops, just run the same command again; it continues where it left off.

Yes, there's one thing to do: run the crawl again once your parse has finished. You did everything right; the 2,496 failures came from a bug in my code, which is now fixed and committed (4a0495e).

What went wrong: cms.tn.gov.in dropped one connection partway through the run. My code then treated that server as down for the rest of the run and marked about 2,380 GOs as permanently failed. The Internet Archive throttled us once, and the same thing happened to Wayback, which caused the 1,363 deferred items.

What changed: - Pausing a server: a server is only paused after 3 failures in a row, and is retried after a cooldown (2 minutes at first, up to 30). - Permanent failure: an item is only marked failed when both the live site and Wayback give a clear "not found". Connection drops, timeouts and throttling leave it pending for the next run. - Your earlier run: the ~2,380 GOs wrongly marked failed will be retried automatically.

All five changes are in and committed (efcb445). All 122 tests pass. I haven't touched the database, because your GO crawl is still running.

What changed: - Per-file progress line: each file now prints one line, e.g. [12:04:31] [137/2385] tn_gos 3f9a…c21 0.84 MB 3s via live If the file wasn't downloaded, the line adds DEFERRED or FETCH_FAILED and the reason. The summary line with time left every 25 files is still there. - Time limit per download: http.max_download_s: 600 in config/settings.yaml. Downloads are streamed and stopped once 600 seconds have passed, even if the server keeps trickling data. A file that arrives shorter than the server announced is also caught. Both count as retryable failures: the item stays pending for the next crawl and shows up as a "retryable fetch failure" in the coverage gap list. - Completeness check: a PDF is kept only if %%EOF is at its end and it opens in PyMuPDF with at least one page. Zero padding after %%EOF is ignored, since one complete GO has 80 KB of it. - Truncated Wayback captures: these no longer count as a newer version under D-018. The crawl tries up to the 3 newest different captures and keeps the newest complete one, recording the skipped ones in the sidecar. Dating still uses the first capture of the bytes actually kept. If none is complete, the item is marked failed. - Existing files: every crawl now starts by checking stored PDFs (once per file). Incomplete ones are moved to data/raw/evidence/_quarantine/, not deleted. Their database entry and chunks are removed, and they're fetched again. - Order: policy notes → GOs → scheme pages → manual → the Wayback-only sources (budget speeches, CAG) last.

What the scan found among the 5,466 PDFs already stored, two incomplete files: - d3b27b7df46eabaf (CAG Report 5 of 2023): your file. Its newest capture (2025) is cut off at exactly 5 MiB, and an older capture from 2024 exists, so the next crawl should replace it with the complete 2024 version. - 2ca1bc0c00d969ae (Industries policy note 2023-24): the server's own file is exactly this size and opens with 241 pages, but it has no %%EOF. Wayback has no copy, so under your rule it becomes a fetch failure. It stays in quarantine either way. Should files like this, complete according to the server and readable, be accepted? Your call; for now the rule is applied as you wrote it.

What to do now: your running crawl --source tn_gos is using the old code. Press Ctrl-C, then run plain:

caffeinate -i python -m ept parse

The crawl first quarantines the two files, then continues with the GOs, scheme pages and finally CAG. Nothing already downloaded is fetched again.

Stage 01 is done and committed as stage 01: corpus collection (675a1c1). All 10 acceptance criteria are met and all 136 tests pass.

Your three answers, applied: 1. Later date wins (D-032). When a GO's own header date is later than its listing date, the header date is stored. On the first try the rule also fired on vague month dates like "June 2024" in the text (193 documents), so I limited it to full dates like "Dated: 23.10.2024". It now changes 49 GOs. In 7 of them OCR probably misread the year: a COVID-19 task-force GO listed in 2021 reads "18.05.2024". Those GOs now show up a few years late in cutoff runs, which loses a little recall but can never leak. They stay flagged in the review sheet. 2. Accepted (D-033). A live PDF without %%EOF is kept if its size matches what the server announced and it opens. The Industries policy note 2023-24 is back in the corpus. This never applies to Wayback copies. 3. Tracker search: six trackers found, four on DMK 2021 and two on AIADMK 2016: South First, Pudhiyavan, an RG Anand PDF, OnlyVotez, and two TNM status checks. None of them cites a GO number. They give verdicts and link to news articles. The leads run found 8 references (6 links to official home pages, 2 Act names), so no documents came in through tracker leads. That makes the planned "with and without tracker leads" comparison in stages 06/07 meaningless unless a better tracker turns up.

Tamil pass (catalogue only, nothing downloaded): 111 Tamil items. 13 are paired with their English version, all budget speeches. The other 98 are Tamil-only candidates: 30 GOs, 58 scheme pages and 10 CAG reports. The English listings link very few Tamil files, and the Tamil-language portal itself is not crawled.

Final corpus: 9,254 documents and 60,259 chunks, with 95.6 % dated to the day. The full report is reports/coverage_01.md.

Two small deviations from the spec, in D-034, for you to check: - The Tamil pairing key includes the speech type, so a Tamil revised speech isn't paired with the English interim speech of the same year. - For a GO lead that isn't in our catalogue, the crawl re-reads that year's GO listings. The spec's extra Wayback search is dropped, because a GO number alone doesn't give the file name to look up. Since no tracker cites GO numbers, this path hasn't run on real data.

Next: stage 02 (promise extraction), in a new conversation, as CLAUDE.md requires. It starts with drafting spec 02: which free-tier model to use, how to split promises, and Tamil manifesto OCR and translation. Tesseract's Tamil language data is already installed on your Mac, so that open question (OQ-6) is answered. One thing to arrange before then: a free-tier LLM API key.

Sources for the trackers: - South First analysis: DMK delivers 394 of 505 poll promises - TNM status check: AIADMK's 2016 promises on water and infrastructure - TNM: Amma housing scheme to free washing machine: AIADMK's social welfare promises - DMK Manifesto 2021 tracker (Pudhiyavan) - DMK's Manifesto Tracker (RG Anand, PDF) - DMK Manifesto Tracker (OnlyVotez)

Global spec, now v0.6. These are the stage 01 results later stages depend on: - §9.1, leakage rules: - Cutoff runs (stage 04) must compare period_end(doc_date, date_precision) with the cutoff, not the stored date. Otherwise a document dated only "2016" (stored as 1 January) would be visible a whole year early. - The realisation-date check (stage 05) works the same way. - §9.3, dates: what doc_date means for every later stage: - the source ranking, with the later of listing and issue date winning (D-032); - Wayback and © year dates being upper bounds, so a document can appear late but never early; - undated documents (220) being left out of every cutoff run; - every questionable date being listed in date_review.csv. - §3.1, Tamil: 98 Tamil-only documents are listed as candidates. Using any of them as evidence still needs a logged decision (D-017). - §9.2, tracker leads: no document came in through trackers, so the "with and without tracker leads" comparison planned for stages 06/07 is trivial. - §2, §5: the environment (Claude Code on your Mac, .venv/, Tamil OCR installed) and the stage 01 commands. - §13, risks: a new risk. Conservative dates can hide evidence at early cutoffs, especially for policy notes and CAG reports, so stage 04 should report how much evidence is available at each cutoff. §13 also records the 193 permanently lost files. - §14: Q-10 notes that Tamil OCR is already available.

- **Two tools, one project folder.** Claude Cowork reads the folder (mounted in its sandbox) and drafts specs, STATUS updates and decision-log entries with the user. Claude Code runs directly on the user's Mac in the project folder and implements, tests and runs the code from the approved spec.

- Network depends on the user's Claude network settings. If an install or fetch fails with a proxy/403 error, report it; don't work around it. Fallback: write the command and the user runs it in their own terminal.

I've read CLAUDE.md, STATUS, the decision log, global spec v0.6 and spec 01's layout, and I looked at all four manifestos. I haven't written or changed anything.

Where we are: stage 01 is done. It's Day 6, and the project is about 2 days behind the day plan, which had stage 02 on Day 5. Stage 02 is meant to settle three open questions: Q-03 (which free LLM to use for bulk work), Q-04 (how to split and de-duplicate promises) and Q-10 (how to handle the Tamil manifestos).

What the manifestos look like

These findings drive most of the plan.

File What it is Text layer Structure
DMK-2021_en.pdf (29 pp) A browser printout of dmk.in Clean English 518 numbered lines covering items 1–505. Five numbers are skipped (18, 80, 136, 251, 441) and 166, 252, 300 appear twice, so they look misnumbered rather than lost. Item 300 also contains a 15-entry railway-route list numbered 1–15. Tamil website menu text is mixed into the lines on some pages, and every page repeats a date/URL header.
DMK-2021_ta.pdf (73 pp) A Word export in a legacy (non-Unicode) font Comes out as garbage 505 numbered items, the same as the English version. Under §3.1 it isn't used for extraction, because an English version exists.
AIADMK-2016_ta.pdf (41 pp) A Word export in a legacy font (VANAVIL family) Comes out as garbage, so it needs tam OCR Numbered section headings with bullets under them. Much of it describes past achievements ("in the last 5 years 3,492 godowns were built") mixed in with the promises.
TVK-2026_ta.pdf (96 pp) Scanned page images at 150 ppi, with colourful design and photos None at all, so it needs tam OCR An introduction, then 10 themed sections (TVK calls them "pillars"). Promise numbering restarts at 1 in each section. Each promise is a red heading followed by a paragraph.

Tesseract tam is only installed on your Mac, so all the OCR runs through Claude Code there.

Plan for spec 02 (global §12.1 template)

Purpose. Turn each term's manifesto into rows in the promises table, with the fields defined in §7 only. The stage 03 fields (sector, type and so on) stay empty.

Inputs. The manifesto PDFs, config/settings.yaml and one prompt file, prompts/extract_promises.md, with a version: header. Language follows §3.1: DMK uses the English file; AIADMK and TVK use the Tamil files with OCR.

Behaviour. ept extract with --term, --limit and --force, and safe to re-run. 1. Page text. Read each page with PyMuPDF and run the stage 01 Tamil-Unicode check. Any page that fails gets Tesseract tam at ocr_dpi. Each page's text is saved to data/interim/manifestos/{term}/, along with how it was read and the OCR confidence. 2. OCR quality check (Q-10). Record each page's confidence and Tamil-character ratio, and flag the worst pages. Proposed accuracy measurement: convert a few pages of the legacy-font text to Unicode with a fixed font mapping and use that as a reference to measure the OCR error rate. This is only a measurement; OCR stays the extraction method. 3. Cutting into units (code, not the LLM). One rule set per manifesto: - DMK: one unit per numbered item. Remove the headers, URLs and menu text. Order goes by position on the page, not by the printed number. A sub-list stays inside its parent item. - AIADMK: section heading, then one unit per bullet. - TVK: section, then one unit per numbered heading plus its paragraph. - Introductions and other front matter are dropped and logged. 4. LLM extraction, one call per page or per batch of units, through ept.llm. The output is a list of {text (English), source_text (verbatim), kind}. kind is promise, past achievement, criticism or statement of values, and only promises are kept. For Tamil, translation happens in the same call. 5. Checks on every promise: - source_text must appear word for word in its page text (ignoring spacing differences). - Every number in text must also appear in source_text. - Latin-script names in text must appear in the source. - One retry, as ept.llm already does; anything that still fails is flagged. 6. Splitting and duplicates (Q-04). Promises split from one manifesto item share a parent_group. Near-duplicates within a term are found by text similarity and handled by the rule you choose (question 4 below). 7. Write the results: - IDs are {term}-{seq:04d} in manifesto order. - A report, reports/extraction_02.md, with counts per term and section, dropped units by reason and OCR statistics. - Run metadata in reports/runs/. - A coverage check: every DMK item from 1 to 505 maps to at least one promise or to a logged exclusion. 8. Bulk LLM test (Q-03). Run 15–20 identical units through each candidate, including Tamil OCR text. Compare how often the JSON is valid, how often the verbatim check passes, translation quality and the rate limits actually hit. Then set llm.models.bulk and implement _bulk.

Leakage warning (rules that apply to this stage). - Use the manifesto text only, with no web search and no model memory. - The English text must not add scheme names, GO numbers, amounts or dates the source doesn't contain. A translation that slips in a later scheme name would leak into stage 03 queries; the step 5 checks are the guard. - Few-shot examples in the prompt are made up, not taken from these manifestos, so they can never collide with the gold set drawn in stage 06. - The same prompt and code are used for all three parties, with the party name passed only as data.

Spot-check (§12.4): 7–10 items in spotcheck_02.csv, at most 3 per term. Ranked by: 1. failed checks; 2. promises from the lowest-confidence OCR pages; 3. odd splits, such as one item producing 4 or more promises, or very short or very long text; 4. dropped units that contain "will" or "shall"; 5. near-duplicates.

Acceptance criteria (draft). 1. Every page has text and a recorded reading method. 2. All Tamil pages pass the Unicode check after OCR. 3. All 3 terms have promises that validate against the schema. 4. Every source_text is verbatim from its page. 5. The number and name checks pass, or each failure has been spot-checked. 6. DMK coverage from 1 to 505 is complete. 7. A re-run makes 0 LLM calls and gives identical output. 8. The report and run metadata exist. 9. The spot-check is done. 10. The tests pass offline.

Tests. Unit cutting for each layout, with fixtures; the verbatim and number checks; removing the menu text; ID order and parent_group; safe re-runs; and a mock LLM.

Out of scope. Stage 03 fields, using the Tamil DMK file for extraction, opposition manifestos and Tamil evidence documents.

Questions for you before I draft the spec

  1. Q-03 backend. I recommend the Gemini free tier as the main option, because it plugs straight into ept.llm. A Kaggle-hosted model would need a file handoff like the strong judge's, and open models are weaker at Tamil. Kaggle would stay as the fallback. Can you get the API key today? The backend test needs it.
  2. Q-04 what counts as a promise. I suggest including "urge the Union government" and "fight against" items, because dropping them would make delivery rates look better than they are; stage 03 marks them union_dependent. Past achievements, criticism of opponents and pure statements of values would be excluded. OK?
  3. Q-04 how fine to split. I suggest splitting only where parts could be delivered and checked separately, such as different beneficiary groups or different amounts. The means stays with its goal: "a committee to draft a state education policy" is one promise. A list such as the 15 railway routes stays one promise. OK?
  4. Q-04 duplicates. The schema has no duplicate field, and adding one would change global §7. I suggest dropping the later duplicate, for example DMK 500 against 498, and listing it in data/interim/promise_dedup.csv. OK?
  5. Q-10 OCR check. Is it OK to use the font-mapping conversion only to measure OCR accuracy? And if it turns out clearly more accurate than OCR on AIADMK, do you want it considered as the main method? That would be a logged departure from §3.1.
  6. Q-10 the 150-ppi TVK scan. If OCR quality falls below a threshold, which fallback do you accept: keep the text and flag the affected promises, or have a vision-capable bulk model read the page images (a logged departure)?
  7. Frozen IDs. Once stage 02 is signed off, promise IDs are frozen, and any later re-extraction needs a decision entry because gold labels will depend on those IDs. OK?

Once you've answered these, I'll draft specs/02-promise-extraction.md.

Turn 34

The delay in following the plan - I'll catch up so don't go cutting anything as of now. The cutting into units part, why are we using different rules for different manifestos? Explain how they are different and why they need to be so. Q03, I have obtained the free API key, but I do not want to share it in chat, how do I let Claude Code access it? Q04, all three are OK. Q10, I feel like font-mapping would work better as trying to do OCR thinking its in a font different from what it actually is seems hard. The fonts used must be some kind of pre-set types, as they all are typed, so I think that would be better. If the quality is low, then we can look towards a vision capable model (we can even use Cowork here to do it). Freeze IDs, OK. Answer my questions, then go on to write up the spec, and any deviations must be aptly modified in the global spec. Update STATUS.md too.

- **Manifestos:** the official English version is used when one exists; otherwise the Tamil version. Tamil PDFs often use legacy (non-Unicode) fonts that extract as garbage, so any page whose extracted text fails a Tamil-Unicode check is OCR'd with Tesseract (`tam`). Extraction (stage 02) produces e …
+++ new
- **Manifestos:** the official English version is used when one exists; otherwise the Tamil version. Each file's text route is set in its layout profile (`config/manifestos.yaml`, spec 02 §4.2):
  - `text_layer`: a clean Unicode text layer (DMK-2021 English).
  - `font_map`: Tamil typed in a **legacy (non-Unicode) font** extracts as garbage, but each glyph maps deterministically to Unicode. Spans in a listed legacy font are converted with the font's mapping table (VANAVIL family, D-035), and fake-bold overprints are removed. This replaces OCR for such fi …
  - `ocr`: image-only pages are OCR'd with Tesseract (`tam`) at native resolution. A quality gate calibrated against font-mapped text sends low-quality pages to **vision transcription** through a Cowork file handoff (§6.4, D-036) (TVK-2026).
  - Every Tamil page must pass a Tamil-share and orthographic-validity check whatever its route.
  - Extraction (stage 02) produces each promise's `text` in English, while `source_text` keeps the original-language span verbatim (Unicode), so every translation can be traced back.

Why the unit-cutting rules differ by manifesto

There is one cutter. The three files just mark "here is a new item" in different ways, so each gets a small layout profile in config/manifestos.yaml saying how:

DMK-2021 (English) AIADMK-2016 (Tamil) TVK-2026 (Tamil)
Where the text comes from Clean text in the PDF Text in an old non-Unicode font, converted to Unicode No text at all (page images), so OCR
How a new item starts N. at the start of a line, running 1–505 A bullet symbol, under numbered section headings A red heading with a number that restarts at 1 in every section
Clutter to remove Browser header and footer, Tamil website menu mixed into lines Every line printed 4 times to fake bold; page headers Footer, photos, colour bands
Special cases Item 300 has its own 1–15 sub-list that must stay inside it Plain paragraphs between bullets, mostly past achievements OCR can miss the white-on-red numbers

A single rule can't work. Cutting on "N." would wreck TVK, where numbers restart, and would never fire on AIADMK's bullets. Sending whole pages instead would cut promises that cross page breaks and would leave the clutter in.

The profiles describe only how each file is laid out. The extraction prompt, the checks and the thresholds are the same for every party (D-040). That matters for neutrality.

There's also a safety net. If no item marker is found, the whole page becomes one unit. The model must copy each promise's original text word for word from the unit, so a weaker cut makes bigger units but not wrong promises.

Giving Claude Code the API key without pasting it

  1. In Terminal: cd ~/Projects/Election-Promise-Tracking && nano .env
  2. Type one line, GEMINI_API_KEY= followed by your key. Save (Ctrl-O, Enter) and exit (Ctrl-X).
  3. Run chmod 600 .env so only your user account can read the file.

.env is already gitignored. The code loads it through ept.config. CLAUDE.md now tells every session never to open, print or commit .env. The key is also kept out of logs, the response cache and run records.

Your other answers, now in the spec and logged

  • Font mapping: you were right. I've updated spec 02 to v0.2 and committed it. OQ-1 and OQ-3 are now settled; the licence is the only question left.

OQ-2: licence

I checked the actual files. The two files that hold the font table (by Arulalan T.) have an explicit GPL v3-or-later notice in their headers. The package's "MIT" label doesn't override that, so the files are GPL.

A disclaimer alone won't settle it. Copying GPL code into your project means anyone who receives the combined program gets GPL rights to it, whatever your own licence says. You have two clean options, and neither costs the half day:

  • (a) GPL v3 for the whole codebase. There's no conflict and nothing extra to manage. This is the simplest.
  • (b) MIT for your own files. The copied file keeps its GPL header, and a THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md says so. This is close to your disclaimer idea, but the notice has to state that the program as shipped with that file is under GPL v3, so in practice MIT only matters for anyone who reuses your files without it.

Either way, the GPL covers code only. Your data (the promise lists and verdicts), the website text and the whitepaper can carry a separate licence such as CC BY 4.0.

I'd pick (a). I'm not a lawyer, so treat this as general information. Tell me (a) or (b) and I'll write it into the spec and finalise it.

OQ-3: done

When a TVK page fails the OCR check, Gemini now reads the page image first. Cowork is used only for pages where Gemini's output still fails the checks (logged as D-042). Gemini models accept image input, and a TVK page costs roughly 1,500 input tokens (Google's docs). The transcription is still compared against the OCR output to catch invented text.

What's wrong with the TVK file

Three things together:

  • No text inside. Each page is a photo-like JPEG, so every word has to be OCR'd.
  • Low resolution. It's 150 ppi; Tesseract works best around 300. Tamil depends on small marks (dots, vowel signs, the pulli), and those blur first at low resolution.
  • Designed layout. Colour bands, photos, and white numbers in red boxes. The OCR may miss those numbers, which mark where each promise starts.

Searching for a better copy is worth it. A properly digital PDF would skip OCR and the quality check entirely. Here's what to look for:

  1. The official source: TVK's website or official social accounts. I found one copy on voterlist.co.in, but that site calls itself unofficial and says the PDF contains "promises made till now", so it may be incomplete. Its robots.txt also stopped me fetching it, so I couldn't check it.
  2. Selectable text: open it in Preview and try to highlight a sentence. If you can, it's digital. If not, check it's sharper than yours: page width of at least about 2,480 px (Tools → Show Inspector).
  3. Complete: about 96 pages, the 10 sections, the same numbering.
  4. An official English version, if one exists. The global spec says to use English whenever there is one.

If you find one, put it in data/raw/manifestos/ and note its URL. The spec now lets a better copy replace the current file any time before the TVK promises are frozen. If nothing turns up, we stay on OCR with Gemini as the fallback.

We're starting the stage 02 build (promise extraction). The spec is approved: specs/02-promise-extraction.md v1.0.

Before writing any code:
1. Read CLAUDE.md, docs/STATUS.md, docs/decisions/log.md (D-035–D-043 are new), specs/00-global-spec.md (v0.7) and specs/02-promise-extraction.md in full.
